name: Video Processing Pipeline
description: Design a video processing and transcoding pipeline like YouTube's backend. Covers upload handling, multi-resolution transcoding, thumbnail generation, CDN delivery, and metadata indexing.

learnSteps.title: Upload Flow with Pre-Signed URLs
learnSteps.description: The client requests an upload URL from the App Server, which generates a pre-signed S3 URL. The client uploads the raw video directly to S3 (bypassing the app server for large files). Once the upload completes, S3 triggers a notification, and the App Server publishes a transcode job to the queue. This pattern avoids bottlenecking the app tier with large file transfers.

learnSteps.title: Multi-Resolution Transcoding Pipeline
learnSteps.description: The Transcode Worker pulls jobs from SQS and runs FFmpeg to produce multiple resolutions (360p, 720p, 1080p, 4K) and formats (H.264, VP9, AV1). Each resolution is a separate output file stored in S3. Workers use spot instances for cost optimization. A single 1-hour 4K video may take 2-6 hours of compute across all output formats.

learnSteps.title: CDN Delivery and Adaptive Bitrate
learnSteps.description: Transcoded videos are served via CloudFront CDN with 200+ edge locations. The player uses HLS/DASH adaptive bitrate streaming — it requests small chunks (2-10 second segments) and switches resolutions based on available bandwidth. Popular videos have high cache hit rates at the edge, reducing origin load and latency.

learnSteps.title: Metadata and Processing State Machine
learnSteps.description: Video metadata (title, duration, resolution, processing status) is tracked in PostgreSQL. The processing state machine: uploaded -> processing -> processed -> published (or failed). The Transcode Worker updates status on completion. The App Server reads this to show upload progress. Eventual consistency is acceptable — the video appears within minutes.

chaosScenarios.name: Spot Instance Reclamation Wave
chaosScenarios.description: A capacity crunch reclaims 40% of the spot-based transcode fleet within minutes, killing in-flight FFmpeg jobs
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: In-flight transcodes die with their instances; their SQS messages reappear after the visibility timeout and restart from scratch on survivors. Queue depth climbs and time-to-publish stretches from minutes to over an hour. No data is lost — raw uploads remain in S3.
mitigationSteps: Diversify the fleet across instance families and AZs to reduce correlated reclamation
Handle the 2-minute interruption notice: stop pulling work and release the current message immediately
Fall back to a bounded on-demand pool when spot capacity drops below 60% of desired
Transcode per-rendition rather than per-video so reclamation loses minutes of work, not hours

chaosScenarios.name: Viral Event Upload Surge
chaosScenarios.description: A breaking-news event triggers a 10x upload spike, flooding the transcode queue far beyond fleet drain capacity
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: SQS absorbs the backlog without loss (queue is the safety valve), but time-to-publish p95 breaches the 10-minute SLO. Upload API remains healthy — pre-signed S3 uploads are unaffected by transcode backpressure.
mitigationSteps: Autoscale the fleet on queue depth, not CPU — depth is the leading indicator
Prioritize the 360p/720p ladder rungs so videos publish fast; backfill 1080p/4K after
Defer non-urgent re-transcode and optimization jobs to a separate low-priority queue
Communicate degraded publish-time expectations via the status API

chaosScenarios.name: Malformed Media File Crash Loop
chaosScenarios.description: An adversarial or corrupt container makes FFmpeg crash or balloon memory (decompression bomb), burning retries across the fleet
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: The job fails on three different workers, consuming worker slots each time, then lands in the DLQ. Memory-bomb variants can OOM the worker and take co-scheduled jobs down with it.
mitigationSteps: Run an ffprobe validation pass before queueing the full transcode; reject unparseable containers at upload
Enforce per-job memory/CPU cgroup limits so one job cannot kill its neighbors
Alert on DLQ arrivals and fingerprint repeat-offender codec paths
Mark the video 'failed' in metadata with a user-visible reason instead of leaving it 'processing'

bottleneckProgression.description: Status writes from workers plus status polls from the app tier exhaust the 300-connection metadata DB pool
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Add PgBouncer, batch worker status updates, and serve status polls from a short-TTL cache

bottleneckProgression.description: Transcode jobs arrive faster than the fleet drains them; backlog and time-to-publish grow without bound
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Scale workers on queue depth with a high max; split renditions into separate messages for finer-grained parallelism

bottleneckProgression.description: Concurrent multipart writes from hundreds of workers hit S3 per-prefix request limits, throttling rendition uploads
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Shard object keys across prefixes (hash-prefixed paths) and tune multipart part sizes

expectedIssues.title: Visibility Timeout Duplicate Transcodes
expectedIssues.description: Long 4K jobs exceed the SQS visibility timeout, so a second worker picks up the same job — duplicate compute and racing S3 writes for identical keys
expectedIssues.mitigation: Heartbeat ChangeMessageVisibility extensions while the job runs; deterministic idempotent output keys so the race is harmless

expectedIssues.title: Status State-Machine Drift
expectedIssues.description: A worker that dies after writing renditions to S3 but before updating PostgreSQL leaves the video stuck in 'processing' forever despite playable output existing
expectedIssues.mitigation: Periodic reconciliation sweep comparing S3 rendition manifests against DB status; auto-complete or requeue divergent records

expectedIssues.title: Transcode Compute Cost Runaway
expectedIssues.description: 4K/AV1 renditions cost 2-6 compute-hours per upload-hour; a sustained upload spike multiplies the largest line item in the budget with no natural cap
expectedIssues.mitigation: Gate expensive renditions (4K, AV1) on view-count thresholds — transcode them lazily only for videos that earn an audience

expectedIssues.title: Cold CDN Misses on Fresh Uploads
expectedIssues.description: The first viewers of every new video miss the CDN and pull from S3 origin, paying 100ms+ extra startup latency exactly when creators are watching their own upload
expectedIssues.mitigation: Accept for the long tail; for subscribed/high-follower creators, pre-warm edge caches on publish

steps: Compare queue arrival rate vs drain rate to size the gap
Check spot fleet health — reclamation looks like a backlog problem from the queue side
Raise max fleet size and add on-demand capacity if spot is constrained
Switch to priority draining: low-res renditions first so videos publish
Pause re-transcode/optimization jobs until backlog clears
Run the reconciliation job: diff S3 rendition manifests against DB status
Auto-complete records whose renditions exist; requeue those with partial output
Inspect worker logs for crash-after-write patterns
Verify the status-update path commits before message ack, not after

runbooks.incident: Repeated FFmpeg crashes on specific files
steps: Pull samples from the DLQ and run ffprobe locally to classify the malformation
Add the failing container/codec signature to upload-time validation
Confirm cgroup memory limits prevented collateral worker damage
Mark affected videos failed with a user-facing reason

decisions.title: Pre-Signed Direct-to-S3 Uploads
decisions.context: Raw video files reach tens of gigabytes; proxying them through the app tier would consume its connections and bandwidth
decisions.decision: App server issues pre-signed S3 URLs and clients upload directly; S3 event notifications trigger the transcode job
consequences: App tier handles only small control-plane requests regardless of file size
Upload availability is S3's availability — better than anything self-hosted
Upload progress and resumability become client+S3 concerns (multipart uploads)

decisions.title: Queue-Decoupled Spot Transcode Fleet
decisions.context: Transcoding is compute-heavy, embarrassingly parallel, and tolerant of minutes of delay — the ideal spot workload
decisions.decision: Buffer all jobs in SQS and process them on a spot fleet sized by queue depth
consequences: Reclamation waves stretch time-to-publish rather than dropping work
Visibility-timeout tuning and idempotent outputs are required correctness work

decisions.title: Progressive Rendition Publishing
decisions.context: Creators expect their video playable in minutes; a full ladder including 4K/AV1 takes hours
decisions.decision: Publish as soon as the first low-res rendition lands; higher tiers and efficient codecs backfill asynchronously
consequences: Time-to-publish SLO measured on 720p, not the full ladder
Early viewers get capped quality briefly
Status model must represent partially-published states

tradeoffs.choice: Spot instances for the transcode fleet
tradeoffs.benefit: The dominant compute line item drops ~70%
tradeoffs.cost: Reclamation waves make time-to-publish a distribution with a long tail, requiring on-demand fallback

tradeoffs.choice: Full multi-codec ladder (H.264, VP9, AV1) stored per video
tradeoffs.benefit: Every device gets an optimal stream; modern codecs cut delivery egress ~30%
tradeoffs.cost: Storage multiplies per codec family; 500TB and growing is the largest budget line

tradeoffs.benefit: Workers never block on coordination; the pipeline is a simple queue-drain loop
tradeoffs.cost: Crash windows create stuck states that need reconciliation sweeps to repair

alternatives.name: Managed Transcode Service (MediaConvert-style)
alternatives.description: Outsource the entire transcode step to a cloud media service
alternatives.prosVsCons: Zero fleet operations and built-in format coverage, but per-minute pricing runs 3-5x a tuned spot fleet at this volume, with less codec/quality control
alternatives.whyNotChosen: At 50-instance sustained scale the cost delta funds the team that runs the fleet; codec tuning is also a product differentiator

alternatives.name: Just-in-Time Transcoding
alternatives.description: Store only the master and transcode renditions on first request per quality level
alternatives.prosVsCons: Massive storage savings on never-watched content, but first-viewer latency in minutes and unpredictable compute spikes
alternatives.whyNotChosen: Unacceptable first-play experience; the hybrid (lazy 4K/AV1 for low-view videos) captures most of the savings

alternatives.name: Synchronous Upload-and-Transcode
alternatives.description: Transcode inline during the upload request and return when the video is ready
alternatives.prosVsCons: Simplest possible state model, but ties up app-tier resources for hours and fails the whole upload on any transcode error
alternatives.whyNotChosen: Multi-hour HTTP requests are a non-starter; decoupling is mandatory at any real scale
